Our department is currently responsible for maintaining 217 parks and a significant amount of acreage across the system. With our existing staffing and operational resources, there are times when we are unfortunately unable to lower flags as quickly as we would like. In addition to flag responsibilities, our crews are balancing a wide range of daily and weekly maintenance and safety related tasks across all of the properties we manage. That said, we recognize the importance of this issue and will look at ways to better reallocate our resources and improve our response time when half-mast directives are issued. While there are operational limitations tied to the size and scope of the system we maintain, we are committed to doing our best to address these concerns moving forward. The best way to get information about Boston's street trees is by going to boston.gov/trees and reading about how to properly request a new street tree, to submit tree maintenance requests, and learn how to care for young street trees. This is done to prevent the trunk of the tree from being damaged by the wet conditions that the watering bag creates around the trunk as well as to encourage new root growth outside of the root ball. Since the watering bag sits on top of the root ball it still waters the tree when it is filled.

Proof should be sent to 1010 Massachusetts Ave Boston, MA 02118 3rd floor. Attn: Urban Forestry Division or emailed to (Trees@boston.gov) Attn: Urban Forestry Division. It should also be noted that tree roots do not have the ability to break into a sewer pipe. They will however grow into an already broken/compromised sewer pipe. Thank you for contacting us regarding the irrigation system and the second watering cycle that occurs around noon. The midday irrigation cycle is intentional and is used only during periods of prolonged heat or unusually dry conditions (June - August). Rather than serving as a full watering, this shorter cycle supplements the early morning irrigation by helping maintain adequate soil moisture and reducing stress on the turf during the hottest part of the day. This is particularly important for recently established turf and heavily used lawn areas. While early morning remains the primary watering time, the additional midday cycle is a temporary measure used to protect the health of the lawn during extreme weather conditions. Once temperatures moderate, the irrigation schedule is adjusted and the supplemental midday watering is discontinued. We appreciate your understanding as we work to maintain healthy, safe, and resilient park landscapes during periods of extreme heat. Sincerely, Boston Parks and Recreation Department

The City of Boston has no authority over trees rooted on private property. Below are a list of suggestions regarding steps you can take to help resolve this issue. 1. Get a Certified Arborist’s Assessment Hiring a Massachusetts Certified Arborist or ISA Certified Arborist can help: • They can provide a written assessment stating whether the tree is hazardous and poses an imminent risk. • You can share that report with your neighbor. 2. Send Written Notice (If the Neighbor Won’t Act) If your neighbor refuses to act after you’ve raised the issue: • You can send a certified letter documenting your concern and warning of potential risk. • Keep a copy — this can protect you later if damage occurs (it shows the neighbor was on notice). 3. Legal Remedies (Last Resort) If the tree clearly endangers your property and the neighbor refuses to act: • You may seek an injunction in District or Superior Court to compel the neighbor to address the hazard. • You can also recover damages if the tree later causes harm and the neighbor had prior notice of the danger.
